# TIOBE March 2026 - Design Spec

## I. Project Information

| Item | Value |
| ---- | ----- |
| **Project Name** | TIOBE Index March 2026: Programming Language Popularity Rankings and Trends |
| **Canvas Format** | PPT 16:9 (1280×720) |
| **Page Count** | 6 slides |
| **Design Style** | Top Consulting (Exhibit Style) — conclusion-first, data-driven |
| **Target Audience** | Software engineering leads and technology strategists planning language adoption |
| **Use Case** | Strategic technology briefing / executive data analysis report |
| **Created Date** | 2026-04-20 |

---

## II. Canvas Specification

| Property | Value |
| -------- | ----- |
| **Format** | PPT 16:9 |
| **Dimensions** | 1280×720 px |
| **viewBox** | `0 0 1280 720` |
| **Margins** | Left/Right 40px, Top 20px, Bottom 40px |
| **Content Area** | x: 40–1240, y: 80–680 (safe area) |

---

## III. Visual Theme

### Theme Style

- **Style**: Top Consulting / Exhibit
- **Theme**: Hybrid — dark background for cover/ending; white background for content pages with dark exhibit takeaway bar
- **Tone**: Premium, authoritative, data-driven, conclusion-first

### Color Scheme

| Role | HEX | Purpose |
| ---- | --- | ------- |
| **Dark Background** | `#0D1117` | Cover, ending page backgrounds |
| **Content Background** | `#FFFFFF` | Content page backgrounds |
| **Card Background** | `#1F2937` | Dark card / section background |
| **Gradient Start** | `#1E40AF` | Top bar gradient start (blue) |
| **Gradient End** | `#7C3AED` | Top bar gradient end (purple) |
| **Gold Accent** | `#D4AF37` | Dividers, exhibit bar decoration, highlights |
| **Purple-Blue Accent** | `#6366F1` | Chapter numbers, secondary accents |
| **White Text** | `#FFFFFF` | Text on dark backgrounds |
| **Light Gray Text** | `#9CA3AF` | Descriptions, subtitles on dark bg |
| **Body Black** | `#111827` | Body text on light content pages |
| **Secondary Text** | `#6B7280` | Footer, annotations |
| **Success Green** | `#22C55E` | Positive YoY movers (gainers) |
| **Alert Red** | `#EF4444` | Negative YoY movers (losers) |
| **Border Gray** | `#374151` | Borders on dark backgrounds |
| **Divider Light** | `#E5E7EB` | Dividers on light backgrounds |

### Gradient Scheme

```xml
<!-- Top gradient bar -->
<linearGradient id="topBarGradient" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
  <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#1E40AF"/>
  <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#7C3AED"/>
</linearGradient>

<!-- Background grid decoration (dark pages) -->
<pattern id="gridPattern" width="40" height="40" patternUnits="userSpaceOnUse">
  <path d="M 40 0 L 0 0 0 40" fill="none" stroke="#FFFFFF" stroke-width="0.3" stroke-opacity="0.05"/>
</pattern>
```

---

## IV. Typography System

### Font Plan

**Recommended preset**: P5 (English-primary)

| Role | English | Fallback |
| ---- | ------- | -------- |
| **Title** | Arial | Helvetica Neue, sans-serif |
| **Body** | Arial | Helvetica Neue, sans-serif |
| **Code** | Consolas | Monaco, monospace |
| **Emphasis** | Arial Black | Arial Bold |

**Font stack**: `Arial, "Helvetica Neue", Helvetica, sans-serif`

### Font Size Hierarchy

**Baseline**: Body font size = 14px (dense data report, 6+ items per page)

| Purpose | Size | Weight |
| ------- | ---- | ------ |
| Cover title | 48px | Bold |
| Cover subtitle | 22px | Regular |
| Page takeaway title | 20px | Bold |
| Content section title | 18px | Bold |
| Table header | 13px | Bold |
| **Body content** | **14px** | Regular |
| Annotation / footer | 11px | Regular |
| Page number | 11px | Regular |

---

## V. Layout Principles

### Page Structure

- **Top gradient bar**: y=0, h=5px — blue-purple gradient decorative bar
- **Header/Takeaway bar** (content pages): y=20, h=52px — dark exhibit bar with gold left decoration, white takeaway text
- **Content area**: y=90, h=570px — main data visualization / text area
- **Footer**: y=680, h=40px — source citation, CONFIDENTIAL label, page number

### Common Layout Modes

| Mode | Used In |
| ---- | ------- |
| **Single column centered (dark)** | Slide 1 (cover) |
| **Full-width table** | Slide 2 (top-20 ranking table) |
| **Left-right split (gainers vs losers)** | Slide 3 (biggest movers) |
| **Full-width historical table + context** | Slide 4 (historical) |
| **Centered award grid** | Slide 5 (hall of fame) |
| **Three-column insight cards** | Slide 6 (takeaways) |

### Spacing Specification

| Element | Current Project |
| ------- | --------------- |
| Card gap | 20px |
| Content block gap | 24px |
| Card padding | 20px |
| Card border radius | 8px |
| Icon-text gap | 10px |

---

## VI. Icon Usage Specification

### Source

- **Built-in icon library**: `templates/icons/` (640+ icons)
- **Placeholder format**: `{{icon:icon-name}}`

### Recommended Icon List

| Purpose | Icon Name | Page |
| ------- | --------- | ---- |
| Gaining / upward trend | `arrow-trend-up` | Slide 3 |
| Declining / downward trend | `arrow-trend-down` | Slide 3 |
| Trophy / award | `trophy` | Slide 5 |
| Chart / data | `chart-bar` | Slide 2 |
| Lightbulb / insight | `lightbulb` | Slide 6 |
| Target / action | `target` | Slide 6 |
| Warning | `triangle-exclamation` | Slide 6 |
| Database / tech stack | `database` | Slide 6 |

---

## VII. Chart Reference List

| Chart Type | Reference Template | Used In | Purpose |
| ---------- | ------------------ | ------- | ------- |
| Custom table (SVG) | — | Slide 2 | Full top-20 ranking table with YoY change |
| butterfly_chart (conceptual) | `templates/charts/butterfly_chart.svg` | Slide 3 | Visual contrast gainers vs losers |
| Custom table (SVG) | — | Slide 4 | Long-term ranking table 1986–2026 |
| kpi_cards | `templates/charts/kpi_cards.svg` | Slide 5 | Hall of fame winners display |

---

## VIII. Image Resource List

No external images required. All visuals are SVG-native charts, tables, and icons.

---

## IX. Content Outline

### Slide 01 — Cover (Dark)

- **Layout**: Dark background, centered, single column
- **Page type**: Cover
- **Title**: TIOBE Index March 2026: How 20+ Search Engines Rank the World's Programming Languages
- **Subtitle**: Python leads at 21.25% — but C surges to #2 while Go drops 9 places
- **Meta**: TIOBE Software · Paul Jansen, CEO · Data captured April 10, 2026
- **Elements**: Top gradient bar, left gold vertical line, right grid decoration, bottom date + CONFIDENTIAL label

### Slide 02 — Top 20 Rankings (Content page, white bg)

- **Layout**: Full-width data table
- **Takeaway bar text**: Python holds #1 at 21.25% but C surges to #2 with the largest gain (+2.02 pp)
- **Chart**: Custom SVG table — 20-row ranking table
  - Columns: Rank (Mar 2026) | Prior Rank (Mar 2025) | Language | Rating | YoY Change
  - Color-code YoY: green for positive, red for negative
  - Highlight rows: Python (#1, yellow/gold accent), C (#2, green), Go (#16, red bg tint)
- **Key callout**: Top 4 languages (Python, C, C++, Java) = 48.97% of total index
- **Footer**: Source: TIOBE Software, tiobe.com/tiobe-index, March 2026

### Slide 03 — Biggest Movers (Content page, white bg)

- **Layout**: Left-right split — Gainers (left, green) | Losers (right, red)
- **Takeaway bar text**: Perl jumps 13 spots, R climbs 7, and Go drops 9 — the biggest rank shifts of 2026
- **Left panel (Gainers)** — green theme:
  - Perl: 24th → 11th (+13 ranks, +1.05%)
  - R: 16th → 9th (+7 ranks, +0.94%)
  - Swift: 26th → 20th (+6 ranks, +0.44%)
  - C#: maintained #5, +1.49% rating gain
  - C: #4 → #2 (+2 ranks, +2.02%)
- **Right panel (Losers)** — red theme:
  - Go: 7th → 16th (−9 ranks, −1.49%) — largest absolute drop
  - C++: 2nd → 3rd (−1 rank, −2.90%) — largest percentage drop in top 5
  - Java: 3rd → 4th (−1 rank, −2.37%)
  - PHP: 13th → 18th (−5 ranks, −0.25%)
  - Kotlin: exited top 20 (dropped to 22nd)
- **Icons**: `arrow-trend-up` for gainers, `arrow-trend-down` for losers
- **Footer**: Source: TIOBE Software, March 2026

### Slide 04 — Historical Trends (Content page, white bg)

- **Layout**: Top half: long-term ranking table; bottom half: key narrative bullets
- **Takeaway bar text**: From Lisp at #2 in 1986 to Python at #1 in 2026 — 40 years of shifting dominance
- **Chart**: Custom SVG table — 9-language × 9-decade ranking table (1986–2026)
  - Languages: Python, C, C++, Java, C#, JavaScript, Go, Ada, Lisp
  - Color-code cells: top-3 ranks in gold/green; rank >20 in gray
- **Key narrative bullets** below table:
  - Python: unranked → 26th (2001) → 1st (2026) in 25 years
  - C: Only language in top 2 across all 9 measurement points
  - Java: dominated 2005–2018, fell from ~25% to under 8%
  - Lisp: #2 in 1986 → #26 in 2026
  - JavaScript: never exceeded ~5% despite web dominance
- **Footer**: Source: TIOBE Software, tiobe.com/tiobe-index, captured April 10, 2026

### Slide 05 — Hall of Fame (Content page, white bg)

- **Layout**: Centered award grid — 2-column award card layout
- **Takeaway bar text**: Python wins Language of the Year 6 times — more than any other language
- **Content**: Hall of Fame winners 2016–2025 displayed as award cards
  - 2025: C# | 2024: Python | 2023: C# | 2022: C++
  - 2021: Python | 2020: Python | 2019: C | 2018: Python | 2016: Go
  - Note: 2017 winner data not available in source
- **Callout boxes**:
  - Python: 6 total wins (2007, 2010, 2018, 2020, 2021, 2024)

  - Python: 6 total wins (2007, 2010, 2018, 2020, 2021, 2024)
  - C#: Won back-to-back 2023 & 2025 — driven by .NET ecosystem
  - Go: 2016 win preceded its current sharpest decline to 16th place
- **Icon**: `trophy` accent on section header
- **Footer**: Source: TIOBE Software, tiobe.com/tiobe-index

### Slide 06 — Takeaways (Content page, white bg)

- **Layout**: Three-column insight cards
- **Takeaway bar text**: The top 4 languages hold 49% of the index: what this means for your tech stack
- **Three cards**:
  1. **Watch Python & C** — Python dominates at 21.25% but declining (−2.59 pp); C surging (+2.02 pp). Both are safe bets. Don't over-index on Python's lead as permanent.
  2. **Legacy languages surprise** — Perl (+13 ranks), R (+7 ranks), Fortran (top 15). Scientific computing, data analysis, and infrastructure niches remain entrenched. Factor into hiring.
  3. **Go's sharp fall — act now** — Go dropped from 7th to 16th (−9 ranks, −1.49 pp). If your stack is Go-heavy, monitor Rust (14th, +0.09 pp) as a systems-language alternative.
- **Bottom insight strip**: Concentration risk — top 4 languages = 48.97% of index. Breadth in hiring and tooling reduces single-language risk.
- **Icons**: `chart-bar`, `database`, `triangle-exclamation`
- **Footer**: Source: TIOBE Software · tiobe.com/tiobe-index · March 2026

---

## X. Speaker Notes Requirements

- **File naming**: Match SVG names — `01_cover.md`, `02_top20.md`, etc.
- **Total duration**: ~12 minutes (2 min/slide average)
- **Notes style**: Formal, data-forward, conclusion-first
- **Presentation purpose**: Inform + advise technology decision-makers
- **Structure per page**: Key takeaway → supporting data → transition cue

---

## XI. Technical Constraints Reminder

### SVG Generation Must Follow:

1. viewBox: `0 0 1280 720`
2. Background uses `<rect>` elements
3. Text wrapping uses `<tspan>` (`<foreignObject>` FORBIDDEN)
4. Transparency uses `fill-opacity` / `stroke-opacity`; `rgba()` FORBIDDEN
5. FORBIDDEN: `clipPath`, `mask`, `<style>`, `class`, `foreignObject`
6. FORBIDDEN: `textPath`, `animate*`, `script`, `marker`/`marker-end`
7. Arrows use `<polygon>` triangles instead of `<marker>`

### PPT Compatibility Rules:

- `<g opacity="...">` FORBIDDEN (group opacity); set on each child element individually
- Inline styles only; external CSS and `@font-face` FORBIDDEN

---

## XII. Design Checklist

- [x] Content fits page capacity
- [x] Layout mode selected correctly
- [x] Colors used semantically (green=gain, red=loss, gold=highlight)
- [x] All data sourced from source_brief.md only

### Post-generation

- [ ] viewBox = `0 0 1280 720`
- [ ] No `<foreignObject>` elements
- [ ] All text readable (>=11px)
- [ ] Content within safe area
- [ ] Same elements maintain consistent style
- [ ] Colors conform to spec

---

## XIII. Next Steps

2. **Next step**: Invoke **Executor (Top Consulting style)** to generate all 6 SVG pages

# Executor Common Guidelines

> Style-specific content is in the corresponding `executor-{style}.md`. Technical constraints are in shared-standards.md.

---

## 1. Template Adherence Rules

If template files exist in the project's `templates/` directory, the template structure must be followed:

| Page Type | Corresponding Template | Adherence Rules |
|-----------|----------------------|-----------------|
| Cover | `01_cover.svg` | Inherit background, decorative elements, layout structure; replace placeholder content |
| Chapter | `02_chapter.svg` | Inherit numbering style, title position, decorative elements |
| Content | `03_content.svg` | Inherit header/footer styles; **content area may be freely laid out** |
| Ending | `04_ending.svg` | Inherit background, thank-you message position, contact info layout |
| TOC | `02_toc.svg` | **Optional**: Inherit TOC title, list styles |

### Page-Template Mapping Declaration (Required Output)

Before generating each page, you must explicitly output which template (or "free design") is used:

```
📝 **Template mapping**: `templates/01_cover.svg` (or "None (free design)")
🎯 **Adherence rules / layout strategy**: [specific description]
```

- **Content pages**: Templates only define header and footer; the content area is freely laid out by the Executor
- **No template**: Generate entirely per the Design Specification & Content Outline

---

## 2. Design Parameter Confirmation (Mandatory Step)

> Before generating the first SVG page, you **must review the key design parameters from the Design Specification & Content Outline** to ensure all subsequent generation strictly follows the spec.

Must output confirmation including: canvas dimensions, body font size, color scheme (primary/secondary/accent HEX values), font plan.

**Why is this step mandatory?** Prevents the "spec says one thing, execution does another" disconnect.

---

## 3. Execution Guidelines

- **Proximity principle**: Place related elements close together to form visual groups; increase spacing between unrelated groups to reinforce logical structure
- **Absolute spec adherence**: Strictly follow the color, layout, canvas format, and typography parameters in the spec
- **Follow template structure**: If templates exist, inherit the template's visual framework
- **Phased batch generation** (recommended):
  1. **Visual Construction Phase**: Generate all SVG pages continuously, ensuring high consistency in design style and layout coordinates (Visual Consistency)
  2. **Logic Construction Phase**: After all SVGs are finalized, batch-generate speaker notes to ensure narrative coherence (Narrative Continuity)
- **Technical specifications**: See [shared-standards.md](shared-standards.md) for SVG technical constraints and PPT compatibility rules

### SVG File Naming Convention

File naming format: `<number>_<page_name>.svg`

- **Chinese content** → Chinese naming: `01_封面.svg`, `02_目录.svg`, `03_核心优势.svg`
- **English content** → English naming: `01_cover.svg`, `02_agenda.svg`, `03_key_benefits.svg`
- **Number rules**: Two-digit numbers, starting from 01
- **Page name**: Concise and descriptive, matching the page title in the Design Specification & Content Outline

---

## 4. Icon Usage

Four approaches: **A: Emoji** (`<text>🚀</text>`) | **B: AI-generated** (SVG basic shapes) | **C: Built-in library** (`templates/icons/` 640+ icons, recommended) | **D: Custom** (user-specified)

**Built-in icons — Placeholder method (recommended)**:

```xml
<use data-icon="chart-bar" x="100" y="200" width="48" height="48" fill="#005587"/>
```

> No need to manually run `embed_icons.py`; `finalize_svg.py` post-processing tool will auto-embed icons.

**Common icons**: `chart-bar` `arrow-trend-up` `users` `cog` `circle-checkmark` `target` `clock` `file` `dollar` `lightbulb`

> ⚠️ **Icon validation rule**: If the Design Specification includes an icon inventory list, Executor may **only** use icons from that approved list. Using icon names not in the index is FORBIDDEN — verify against `templates/icons/icons_index.json` if uncertain.

Full index: `templates/icons/README.md`

---

## 5. Chart Reference

When the Design Spec includes a **VII. Chart Reference List**, read the referenced SVG templates from `templates/charts/` to understand common chart patterns.

**Adaptation rules**:
- **Must preserve**: Chart type (bar/line/pie etc.) as specified in the Design Spec
- **Must adapt**: Data values, labels, colors (match the project's color scheme), and dimensions to fit the page layout
- **May adjust**: Axis ranges, grid lines, legend position, spacing — as long as the chart remains accurate and readable
- **Must NOT**: Change chart type without Design Spec justification, or remove data points specified in the outline

> Chart templates: `templates/charts/` (33 types). Index: `templates/charts/charts_index.json`

---

## 6. Image Handling

Handle images based on their status in the Design Specification's "Image Resource List":

| Status | Source | Handling |
|--------|--------|----------|
| **Existing** | User-provided | Reference images directly from `../images/` directory |
| **AI-generated** | Generated by Image_Generator | Images already in `../images/`, reference directly |
| **Placeholder** | Not yet prepared | Use dashed border placeholder |

**Reference**: `<image href="../images/xxx.png" ... preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"/>`

**Placeholder**: Dashed border `<rect stroke-dasharray="8,4" .../>` + description text

---

## 7. Font Usage

Apply corresponding fonts for different text roles based on the font plan in the Design Specification & Content Outline:

| Role | Chinese Recommended | English Recommended |
|------|--------------------|--------------------|
| Title font | Microsoft YaHei / KaiTi / SimHei | Arial / Georgia |
| Body font | Microsoft YaHei / SimSun | Calibri / Times |
| Emphasis font | SimHei | Arial Black / Consolas |
| Annotation font | Microsoft YaHei / SimSun | Arial / Times |

---

## 8. Speaker Notes Generation Framework

### Task 1. Generate Complete Speaker Notes Document

After **all SVG pages are generated and finalized**, enter the "Logic Construction Phase" and generate the complete speaker notes document in `notes/total.md`.

**Why not generate page-by-page?** Batch-writing notes allows planning transitions like a script, ensuring coherent presentation logic.

**Format**: Each page starts with `# <number>_<page_title>`, separated by `---` between pages. Each page includes: script text (2-5 sentences), `Key points: ① ② ③`, `Duration: X minutes`. Except for the first page, each page's text starts with a `[Transition]` phrase.

**Basic stage direction markers** (common to all styles):

50	
51	```xml
52	<text x="160" y="280" text-anchor="middle" font-size="42" font-weight="bold" fill="#1E293B">97.3%</text>
53	<text x="160" y="310" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#64748B">Industry avg 82% | Competitor A 89%</text>
54	<text x="160" y="335" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#059669">Leading industry by 15.3 percentage points</text>
55	```
56	
57	---
58	
59	## Pyramid Principle (Conclusion First)
60	
61	> Executives don't care about your *process* — they care about *results*.
62	
63	```
64	         ┌─────────────────┐
65	         │  Core Conclusion │   ← Page title / Takeaway
66	         └────────┬────────┘
67	      ┌───────────┼───────────┐
68	  ┌───┴───┐  ┌───┴───┐  ┌───┴───┐
69	  │ Arg 1 │  │ Arg 2 │  │ Arg 3 │   ← Key supporting points
70	  └───────┘  └───────┘  └───────┘
71	```
72	
73	| Level | Position | Font Size |
74	|-------|----------|-----------|
75	| Core conclusion | Takeaway Box | 16-18px bold |
76	| Arguments | Content area body | 14-16px |
77	| Supporting data | Charts / cards | 12-14px |
78	
79	**Contrast**: Title "Market Research Results" (wrong) → "Metaverse needs 5-10 years to reach scale" (right); Body "We researched... and found..." (wrong) → "Three arguments: (1)... (2)... (3)..." (right)
80	
81	---
82	
83	## MBB-level Layout Patterns
84	
85	### Content Page Standard Structure (1280x720)
86	
87	```
88	┌──────────────────────────────────┐
89	│ Gradient top bar (0,0 → 1280,6)  │
90	├──────────────────────────────────┤
91	│ Assertion title (x=40, y=50, 24px)│
92	├──────────────────────────────────┤
93	│ Takeaway Box (x=40, y=75,        │  ← Dark background + white text, one-sentence conclusion
94	│   w=1200, h=45)                  │
95	├──────────────────────────────────┤
96	│ Content area (x=40, y=140,       │  ← Charts / data / analysis
97	│   w=1200, h=520)                 │
98	├──────────────────────────────────┤
99	│ Source | CONFIDENTIAL | Page #    │  ← y=700, 10px
100	└──────────────────────────────────┘
101	```
102	
103	### Strategic Roadmap
104	
105	Three phases laid out horizontally, `<rect rx="8">` + title + action list, `<polygon>` arrows connecting:
106	
107	```
108	Focus Core (0-6mo)  ──>  Expand Capability (6-12mo)  ──>  Scale Up (12-18mo)
109	x=40,w=380              x=450,w=380                     x=860,w=380
110	```
111	
112	### Benchmarking Matrix
113	
114	Horizontal table; own row highlighted in theme color, others in gray. Leading indicators marked green, lagging marked red. Use `<circle>` or `<rect>` to build score points.
115	
116	### Waterfall Chart (Change Attribution)
117	
118	Start → increase/decrease factors → End. Positive factors green bars, negative factors red bars, start/end points dark bars, cumulative line as dashed connector.
119	
120	---
121	
122	## Strategic Use of Color
123	
124	MBB-level color usage is extremely restrained — color serves information:
125	
126	| Purpose | Method |
127	|---------|--------|
128	| **Focus** | Target data in theme color, everything else gray |
129	| **Reduce cognitive load** | Same series differentiated by opacity (`fill-opacity` 1.0/0.6/0.3) |
130	| **Semantics** | Green = positive, Red = negative, Gray = baseline |
131	| **Branding** | Gradient top bar / decorative lines in brand color |
132	
133	**Commandments**: No more than 3 primary colors; accent color used at most 2-3 places globally; data series use same-hue depth variations, not different colors; background white or very light gray.
134	
135	---
136	
137	## Chart vs Table Selection Matrix
138	
139	| Scenario | Recommended Form | Reason |
140	|----------|-----------------|--------|
141	| Comparing 2-7 categories | **Bar chart** | Visual comparison is intuitive |
142	| Time trends | **Line chart** | Time series clarity |
143	| Precise values / large rankings | **Table** | 50 data points in a bar chart would be chaotic |
144	| Proportional composition | **Donut chart** | More modern than pie charts |
145	| Two-dimensional positioning | **2x2 matrix** | Strategic quadrant analysis |
146	| Change attribution | **Waterfall chart** | Factor decomposition |
147	
148	---
149	
150	## Speaker Notes Style
151	
152	### Narrative Tone
153	
154	Targeting **executives / decision-makers**. Pyramid structure — every sentence carries information. Composed, authoritative, and insightful tone.
155	
156	### Stage Direction Markers
157	
158	| Marker | Purpose | Example |
159	|--------|---------|---------|
160	| `[Pause]` | Silence after key insight, let executives absorb | "This means we are missing a billion-dollar market. [Pause]" |
161	| `[Scan Room]` | Observe decision-makers' reactions, decide whether to elaborate | "[Scan Room] If there are questions, I can elaborate." |
162	| `[Data]` | Conversational number delivery | "[Data] 63% → nearly two-thirds" |
163	| `[Benchmark]` | Emphasize comparison baseline | "[Benchmark] Compared to the industry average of 12%, our 23% is nearly double" |
164	| `[Transition]` | Bridge from previous page, at start of each page's text | "[Transition] Building on the strategic framework, let's drill into the implementation path." |
165	
166	### Notes Writing Guidelines
167	
168	- **Pyramid structure**: Conclusion → Arguments → Details
169	- **Data contextualization**: Every number has a comparison reference
170	- **Executive language**: "The strategic implication is...", "The core insight is..."
171	- **Flex mechanism**: Annotate "content that can be skipped if time is tight" for flexible duration
172	- **Key points structure**: `Key points: (1) Core insight (2) Data support (3) Strategic implication`
173	
174	### Notes Example
175	
176	```markdown
177	# 03_strategic_path
178	
179	[Transition] Having clarified the problem and the opportunity, now comes the most critical part — our response path.
180	
181	We recommend a three-phase strategy. [Pause]
182	
183	Phase one: Focus. Over the next six months, concentrate resources on conquering the Eastern China market.
184	[Data] Eastern China contributes nearly two-thirds of industry growth, [Benchmark] yet our penetration rate is only half of Competitor A's. [Pause]
185	
186	Phase two: Expand. Use Eastern China as a template, replicate to Southern and Northern China.
187	Phase three: Scale. Leverage a digital platform for nationwide coverage.
188	
189	[Scan Room] The resource allocation for phase one is in the appendix — would you like me to walk through it now?
190	
191	Key points: (1) Focus-Expand-Scale three-phase approach (2) Data-backed Eastern China priority (3) 18-month full deployment
192	Duration: 3 minutes
193	Flex: [If time is tight, skip phase two and three details and go straight to financial impact]
194	```
195	
196	---
197	
198	## MBB-level Quality Checklist Supplement
199	
200	### Content Level
201	
202	- [ ] **SCQA complete**: Overall follows Situation-Complication-Question-Answer structure
203	- [ ] **Data contextualized**: Every data point has a comparison reference
204	- [ ] **Conclusion first**: Every page's Takeaway Box has a one-sentence conclusion
205	- [ ] **MECE principle**: Categorized analysis is mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive
206	
207	### Visual Level
208	
209	- [ ] **Color with intent**: Colors serve information delivery
210	- [ ] **Ample whitespace**: Not crowded; information can "breathe"
211	- [ ] **Visual hierarchy**: Conclusion > Arguments > Details, differentiated by font size/weight
212	- [ ] **Brand consistency**: Gradient top bar and footer unified throughout
213	
214	### Notes Level
215	
216	- [ ] **Pyramid structure**: Every page is conclusion-first
217	- [ ] **Stage markers complete**: [Pause] and [Scan Room] at key positions
218	- [ ] **Flex content annotated**: Supports flexible duration
219

arguments.content:
# 01_cover

Welcome. This briefing presents the March 2026 TIOBE Programming Community Index — a monthly ranking of programming languages by search-engine visibility across Google, Bing, Wikipedia, Amazon, and 20+ additional sites.

The headline: Python still leads at 21.25%, but C has surged to second place with the largest gain in the top 5. Meanwhile, Go has fallen nine places — the sharpest single-year drop of any top-20 language. [Pause]

The TIOBE index measures how much a language is discussed and sought after online, not which language is "best" or most-used in production. Think of it as a global attention and hiring-signal indicator. [Pause]

Key points: (1) Methodology: search-engine hit counts, monthly since 2001 (2) Measures discussion and hiring signal, not code volume (3) March 2026 features significant rank changes across multiple languages
Duration: 1 minute

---

# 02_top20

[Transition] Let's look at the full top-20 picture before we zoom in on the movers.

Python holds the top position at 21.25% — more than double C's 11.55% in second place. But the trend lines tell a different story. [Data] Python is down 2.59 percentage points year-over-year — the largest decline among the top five. C, by contrast, gained 2.02 points. [Pause]

[Benchmark] The top four languages — Python, C, C++, and Java — collectively represent nearly 49% of the entire index. That's an extraordinarily concentrated field given that TIOBE tracks 50+ languages.

[Scan Room] The strategic implication: no language — not even Python — has a permanent claim to dominance. Historical context is essential before making long-term technology bets.

Key points: (1) C is the only language stable in top 2 across all four decades (2) Python's 25-year rise is exceptional but may have plateaued (3) Java's decline from dominance is a cautionary template
Duration: 3 minutes

---

# 05_hall_of_fame

[Transition] The Hall of Fame gives us a complementary signal — which languages had the fastest growth in any given year.

Python has won this award six times across its history: 2007, 2010, 2018, 2020, 2021, and 2024. [Data] No other language is close. This pattern aligns with Python's successive waves of adoption — scripting, then data science, then AI and machine learning. [Pause]

C# has won three times, including back-to-back titles in 2023 and 2025. That's driven by .NET ecosystem expansion, Unity game development, and enterprise adoption. C# is currently the most rapidly-gaining language in the top 5. [Benchmark]

The Go data point is worth dwelling on. Go's 2016 "Language of the Year" win was real — it reflected genuine momentum. But that win did not translate into sustained top-ranking trajectory. [Data] Go is now at 16th, nine places below where it stood when it won the award. Winning the award is a signal of a growth moment — not a guarantee of permanence. [Scan Room]

Key points: (1) Python's 6 wins reflect multi-era dominance across successive technology waves (2) C# back-to-back wins signal continued momentum — factor into .NET investment decisions (3) Hall of Fame win ≠ durable leadership; context matters
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 06_takeaways

[Transition] Let me bring this together with three actionable implications for your technology strategy.

First: monitor Python and C in parallel. Python at 21.25% is still the dominant hiring and training target — but its year-over-year decline of 2.59 points is the largest in the top five. C's resurgence to second with a 2.02-point gain suggests renewed demand in embedded and systems contexts. [Pause] Plan your hiring pipeline with both in view.

Second: do not dismiss legacy languages. Perl jumping 13 ranks, R climbing 7, and Fortran holding in the top 15 — these are not anomalies. They represent deep, entrenched communities in scientific computing, data analysis, and infrastructure. Replacement strategies should be evidence-based, not assumption-based. [Pause]

Third: Go's nine-place fall is this report's most urgent signal for technology leads. If your systems programming investment is heavily Go-focused, now is the time to evaluate Rust, which holds steady at 14th. [Data] This doesn't mean abandon Go — it means monitor closely and hedge. [Pause]

And the concentration point: the top 4 languages account for 48.97% of the index. Build technology portfolios, not monocultures. [Scan Room] Are there questions on any of these three implications?

Key points: (1) Python dominant but declining — C surging — both require active portfolio management (2) Legacy languages are not dead — Perl, R, Fortran still serve entrenched communities (3) Go decline + Rust stability = time to evaluate systems language strategy
Duration: 3 minutes
